texts.0: SP, due to joining the initial straight off the navigation route without levelling at the briefed pattern altitude, arrived at the break point with an uncontrolled vertical trend. Break altitude deviated beyond 300 feet and the trend continued through the roll. The IP intervened on the controls to reposition the aircraft in the break zone at the correct altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction during the recovery to the field, allowed the aircraft to leave the briefed pattern altitude before the break point. Break altitude reached the 300 feet limit and was corrected only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. The briefed altitude was regained late, well into the turn to downwind.
texts.2: SP, due to changing pitch attitude before the power was set on the initial, allowed break altitude to leave the 150 feet band. The deviation reached approximately 250 feet before SP identified it on the altimeter and re-established the briefed altitude unaided. The correction was complete before roll-out on downwind.
texts.3: SP levelled off from the navigation recovery and flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude, with deviations held inside 150 feet through the roll and the deceleration. Power and pitch were set before the break point, so no vertical excursion developed. Altitude control required no prompting at any stage.
texts.4: SP arrived at the initial already stabilized and completed the break with altitude deviations barely readable on the altimeter. Pitch, power and trim were set ahead of the break point, so the roll was flown with no correction required at all.
texts.marginal: SP held break altitude within the required standard, but the deviations sat near the outer edge of the 150 feet band on each pattern and always in the climbing sense. The tendency is to let the nose rise as bank is applied at the break point. SP is expected to complete the level-off and trim the aircraft earlier on the initial so that altitude is captured before the break.

texts_at.0: With the IP flying the break and calling out the pitch and power changes, SP followed on the controls through the roll into the descending turn and began comparing the altimeter with the briefed pattern altitude. Recognizing and correcting a developing altitude trend during the break has not yet been asked of SP, so the level-off still depends on the IP's timing. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin naming the altitude trend on the early passes before taking over the correction independently.
texts_at.1: SP held break altitude inside the tolerance required at this stage of training, with the deviation settling at about 300 feet as bank was applied at the break point. The trend comes from a slight nose-up tendency during the roll-in that is corrected only after the fact rather than anticipated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to trim for level flight before initiating the roll-in so the altitude does not need a late correction.
texts_at.2: SP kept break altitude inside the tolerance required at this stage, with the excursion settling at about 220 feet as pitch attitude changed ahead of the power setting. The deviation traces to a pitch change begun slightly before the power reduction rather than together with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set pitch and power together at the break point so the excursion narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP held break altitude within about 150 feet of the briefed pattern altitude, with the small excursion tracing to power being set a beat after the pitch change rather than together with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to coordinate pitch and power at the break point so that even this small excursion is removed.

Trimming for level flight a little earlier on the initial would leave less to correct at the break point. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.

Setting pitch and power together at the roll-in would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good break altitude control.

This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good break altitude control.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at the initial already stabilized and completed the break with altitude deviations of only a few tens of feet, with pitch, power and trim all set ahead of the break point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent break altitude control.

The excessive bank was not reduced as the turn progressed and produced downwind spacing that could not be recovered. The IP took control to unload the aircraft and re-establish the briefed bank.
texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored roll rate at the break point, applied a bank that reached the 15 degrees deviation limit from the briefed value. The bank was reduced only after the IP called the attitude, and the correct value was re-established late in the turn. Downwind spacing had to be adjusted as a result.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll input applied faster than briefed, allowed break bank to deviate past the 10 degrees band. The deviation reached approximately 13 degrees before SP cross-checked the attitude indicator and set the briefed bank without assistance. Downwind spacing was unaffected.
texts.3: SP established the briefed break bank promptly and held it within 10 degrees throughout the turn. The roll rate was smooth and the bank was cross-checked against the attitude indicator, producing the planned downwind spacing.
texts.4: SP set the briefed break bank in a single smooth input and held it with deviations not measurable on the attitude indicator. The resulting downwind spacing matched the briefed value with no adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP kept break bank within the required standard, but the values sat consistently at the shallow edge of the 10 degrees band. The tendency is to under-bank at the break and then add a second correcting input. SP is expected to establish the briefed bank in one deliberate roll and confirm it on the attitude indicator.

texts_at.3: SP held break bank at about 8 degrees through the turn, with the small variation tracing to a brief pause in the roll-in while the horizon reference was checked. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to continue the roll to the target bank without an intervening pause.

texts_above.2: SP established the briefed break bank promptly and cross-checked it against the attitude indicator, holding about 12 degrees for the turn. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound bank control through the break.

error_modes.label: Downwind airspeed and minimum speed compliance

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed after the navigation recovery, allowed downwind speed to fall below the 120 KIAS minimum and to exceed the tolerance by more than 20 knots high earlier in the leg. Neither excursion was recognized from the airspeed indicator. The IP intervened on the throttle to restore the briefed downwind speed.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check while the landing checks were being run, allowed downwind airspeed to reach the plus 20 knots limit of the tolerance. The speed was reduced only after the IP called it, and the briefed value was regained late in the leg. The minimum of 120 KIAS was maintained throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after the break, allowed downwind airspeed to leave the plus 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 17 knots before SP cross-checked the airspeed indicator and set the briefed speed unaided, with the minimum of 120 KIAS never approached.
texts.3: SP placed the aircraft on downwind at the briefed speed with no value below the 120 KIAS minimum and no excess beyond 10 knots. The airspeed indicator was included in a continuous cross-check while the checks were run, so power adjustments were small and timely.
texts.4: SP set downwind airspeed at the briefed value immediately after the break and held it with excursions that were not measurable on the indicator. Speed remained clear of the 120 KIAS minimum at all times and no power correction was needed after the initial setting.
texts.marginal: SP kept downwind airspeed within the required standard, but the values sat at the top of the plus 10 knots band for most of the leg. The tendency is to carry surplus energy from the recovery into the pattern and bleed it off late. SP is expected to cross-check airspeed at fixed points on downwind and set the briefed value before the abeam position.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the airspeed and the power changes needed after the break, SP followed on the throttle while beginning to include the airspeed indicator in the cross-check during the landing checks. Managing downwind airspeed and the 120 KIAS minimum through the checks without prompting has not yet been asked of SP. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin cross-checking airspeed at fixed points on downwind before the IP's calls are needed.
texts_at.1: SP held downwind airspeed inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 20 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum after the break. The margin traces to surplus energy carried from the recovery that is bled off gradually rather than set with an early power reduction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power promptly after the break so the margin above the minimum narrows sooner.
texts_at.2: SP kept downwind airspeed inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 14 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum. The margin traces to a power reduction made in two steps rather than set once after the break. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the downwind power in a single reduction so the margin above the minimum tightens further.
texts_at.3: SP held downwind airspeed at about 10 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum for most of the leg, the small margin tracing to a power setting read from feel rather than confirmed on the gauge immediately after the break. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm the power setting on the gauge at the break so the margin above the minimum is set precisely.

texts_above.1: SP held downwind airspeed to about 19 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum through the landing checks, the correction following a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP cross-checked the airspeed indicator through the landing checks and settled downwind speed at about 14 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum without prompting. Setting the downwind power in one reduction after the break, rather than two, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady downwind airspeed control.
texts_above.3: SP placed the aircraft on downwind at about 7 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum by setting power once, immediately after the break, and held it there through the landing checks. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate downwind airspeed control.
texts_above.4: SP set downwind airspeed immediately after the break and held it with excursions of only a knot or two above the 120 KIAS minimum for the whole leg, needing no power correction after the initial setting. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary downwind airspeed control.

texts.0: SP, due to leaving power set for downwind while the descending turn was established, allowed base leg airspeed to exceed the tolerance by more than 20 knots. The excess was carried through the turn and left the aircraft high and fast at the roll-out point. The IP intervened on the throttle and controls to salvage the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction entering base, allowed base leg airspeed to reach the plus 20 knots limit. The speed was reduced only after repeated calls from the IP, and the briefed value was not regained until the aircraft was almost on final.
texts.2: SP, due to an increased descent rate in the turn without a matching power change, allowed base leg airspeed to leave the plus 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 16 knots before SP identified it and set the briefed speed unaided, with the correction complete before roll-out on final.
texts.3: SP established the briefed base leg speed at the start of the turn and held it within 10 knots to roll-out. Power and pitch were coordinated through the descending turn, so no speed excursion developed and the speed never fell below the briefed value.
texts.4: SP flew the base leg at the briefed speed with excursions that were not readable on the airspeed indicator. Power was set once at the start of the turn and the descending turn required no further speed correction.
texts.marginal: SP held base leg airspeed within the required standard, but the values sat at the upper edge of the plus 10 knots band throughout the turn. The tendency is to enter base with surplus speed and rely on the turn to bleed it off. SP is expected to set the briefed base leg power before starting the turn so the speed is stable from the beginning of the descent.

texts_at.0: With the IP setting the base leg power and calling the airspeed through the descending turn, SP followed on the controls while beginning to divide attention between the turn and the airspeed indicator. Coordinating power and pitch through the turn to base without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin reducing power at the start of the turn without the IP's call before holding the speed unaided.
texts_at.1: SP held base leg airspeed inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 20 knots above the briefed value through the descending turn. The margin traces to power being left at the downwind setting into the turn rather than reduced with the descent. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power at the start of the turn to base so the margin narrows from the beginning of the descent.
texts_at.2: SP kept base leg airspeed inside the tolerance required at this stage, settling at about 14 knots above the briefed value through the turn. The margin traces to a power reduction started a beat after the descent was established rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power at the same moment the descending turn is started so the margin tightens further.
texts_at.3: SP held base leg airspeed at about 10 knots above the briefed value for the turn, the small margin tracing to pitch and power being coordinated slightly after roll-in rather than together with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to coordinate pitch and power with the roll-in so the margin narrows to the briefed value.

texts_above.1: SP held base leg airspeed to about 19 knots above the briefed value through the descending turn, the correction following a verbal call from the IP. Reducing power at the same moment the turn to base begins, rather than a beat later, would leave less to correct. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the surplus speed entering the turn to base and reduced it to about 14 knots above the briefed value without prompting, well before roll-out on final. Reducing power at the moment the turn begins, rather than a beat later, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable base leg speed control.
texts_above.3: SP established the briefed base leg speed at the start of the turn and held it to within about 7 knots for the whole descending turn by coordinating pitch and power with the roll-in. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good base leg speed control.
texts_above.4: SP flew the base leg at the briefed speed with excursions of only a knot or two, power set once at the start of the turn with no further correction needed through the descent. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior base leg speed control.

Neither excursion was corrected as the runway was approached. The IP took control to re-establish the aircraft on the correct profile.

texts.2: SP, due to an under-planned roll-out point, arrived on final above the plus 100 feet band by approximately 160 feet. SP recognized the high profile on the visual references, adjusted power and pitch and re-established the correct glidepath before the aircraft reached the threshold area, without any assistance.
texts.3: SP rolled out on final on profile and held the glidepath within 100 feet high and 50 feet low to the threshold. The roll-out point was planned so that no large correction was required, and small power adjustments kept the aircraft on the correct descent path.
texts.4: SP arrived on final exactly on profile and flew the glidepath with deviations that were barely readable. The descent path was held with minimal power adjustments and the aircraft crossed the threshold area precisely on profile.

The tendency is to plan the roll-out point slightly late and remain high to the threshold. SP is expected to start the base descent earlier so that the aircraft is on profile at roll-out rather than correcting down the final.

The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin naming the profile out loud on final before planning the roll-out point independently.
texts_at.1: SP held the final profile inside the tolerance required at this stage, arriving on final about 190 feet high before returning to the glidepath. The excursion traces to a roll-out point planned a little inside the one that matches the descent already established on base. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to plan the roll-out point further out so the aircraft joins closer to the glidepath initially.
texts_at.2: SP kept the final profile inside the tolerance required at this stage, arriving about 155 feet high before settling onto the glidepath. The excursion traces to the base descent being started a few seconds later than the roll-out point required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the base descent at the point that matches the planned roll-out so the initial excursion narrows further.
texts_at.3: SP arrived on final about 80 feet high of the glidepath before the small excursion was absorbed with a minor power adjustment, tracing to a roll-out point planned a few seconds later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to plan the roll-out point precisely from the base descent so this small excursion is removed.

Planning the roll-out point from the base descent, rather than a little inside it, would settle the profile with less correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the high profile on the visual references and reduced the excursion to about 155 feet before the aircraft reached the threshold area, without prompting. Starting the base descent at the point that matches the planned roll-out, rather than a few seconds later, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured glidepath control on final.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on final close to profile and held the glidepath within about 80 feet high to the threshold, the roll-out point planned so that only small power adjustments were needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise glidepath control on final.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate glidepath control on final.

texts.0: SP, due to flying the AOA pattern on airspeed alone without referring to the AOA indexer, allowed AOA to deviate beyond 3 units from the briefed value on base and final. The high AOA excursion was allowed to develop into the onset of buffet. The IP intervened on the controls to reduce the angle of attack.

texts.2: SP, due to a pitch change made without a matching power adjustment, allowed AOA to leave the 1.5 units band on downwind. The deviation reached approximately 2.5 units before SP referred to the indexer and re-established the briefed AOA unaided before the turn to base.
texts.3: SP flew the AOA pattern with the indexer within 1.5 units of the briefed value on downwind, base and final. AOA was cross-checked continuously against airspeed and attitude, so pitch and power corrections were small and timely throughout.
texts.4: SP held the briefed AOA on downwind, base and final with deviations that were barely perceptible on the indexer. The correct angle of attack was maintained through both the configuration changes and the descending turn without any correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept AOA inside the required standard, but the indications sat at the high edge of the 1.5 units band through the base turn. The tendency is to add back pressure in the turn and then reduce it on final. SP is expected to keep the AOA indexer in the primary scan through the turn and to control angle of attack with power rather than pitch alone.
